title: Warehouse worker, 8 games in 2 months, I design everything and AI writes all the code
author: Junior_Muffin5931
selftext:
Been lurking for a while, figured it's time to share what I've been building. Since early October I've been vibe coding games while working full time in a warehouse. I design everything, every mechanic, rule and number, and AI writes all the code. I started on ChatGPT and Codex, and now Claude does most of the work. My setup is scheduled coding sessions that run every hour during the day while I'm at work, each one coding for 30 minutes, pushing to GitHub, running the tests and sending me a short summary plus questions. Builds land on my phone daily and I test everything there.

It started with ADHD Pixel Dungeon (APD). In early October I forked Shattered Pixel Dungeon, which is open source, and started building my own version. October 16 I sent the first alpha to 21 testers. Since then it's grown a full Community side with run submissions, voting and weekly tournaments, a run review system where other players replay your exact run to judge it, and a Lua mod system in the works. November 18 it went into Google Play's closed test, and it launches on Google Play January 1, 2027.

October 8 I came up with President of the Office, an incremental where you're the president and your whole goal is to golf while the government runs around you. Keep Political Capital and Approval up or you get impeached, and win re-election on a real state by state map. The balance gets tuned by headless sims running thousands of simulated hours. Target is February 15, 2027.

Monster Civilization started October 20, and the origin is kind of dumb. I'd just hit a deer with my car and was talking to GPT to calm down. I asked it for APD ideas and it threw out a necromancer class. That turned into what if you played as the monsters instead, like a rat flipping the dungeon around and hunting the hero. Then it became a whole settlement of monsters sending out expeditions, then generations of monsters being born, growing up, picking careers, getting better at whatever they actually do, and dying. By then it was way too big for APD, so it became its own game. Every birth, death, fight and famine has a cause you can trace back. Biggest lesson from this one: GPT had quietly built it as a website inside an app. It's getting a native Kotlin port where every piece has to match the old version bit for bit before it counts. It's going PC first on Steam Early Access, target July 1, 2027, mobile after.

Right at the start of November I also built an unofficial Android port of Trimps, one of my all time favorite incrementals. Original game, original mechanics, mobile UI and save import so I could bring over my Zone 721 Steam save. The creator gave me the okay to put it on Google Play as long as it's clearly labeled unofficial. Now it's getting rewritten as a true native app, and it has to produce the exact same results as the original on my late game saves before it ships.

Tenths started November 3. It's a racing team manager where you design the car, run the factory and make the calls live during the race on a 2D track. Same story as MC, it was a web view, so it's being ported to true native Kotlin with the same bit for bit rule. 23.9 million values checked and identical so far. Public target is April 15, 2027.

November 19 I started two more. Recurrence is an incremental where the universe keeps ending and restarting, nothing is random, and you're the only thing that remembers each loop. All 10 eras are built. Target March 15, 2027. Starcats is a deep idle game about space cats breeding, gearing up and fighting across the stars, with supernovas, expeditions and challenges. Target May 15, 2027.

Newest is Lantern March, started November 24, a roguelike tower defense for mobile where the road keeps growing as you play. Target May 1, 2027.

Also built my studio site, charltonborn-studios.com, and the Cloudflare server that runs APD's online features. Biggest takeaways: write down every rule you care about, because the AI will forget or take shortcuts if you don't. Don't trust "done" until you've seen it on your own device. And make it ask you questions instead of guessing.

comments.author: StaticAnchor
comments.body:
I’m saying this from a place of love, and someone who’s also prototyped 10 games in 2 months.

Slow down.

I realized how thin I spread myself. Genuinely good ideas but the next idea lit me up. You probably have ADHD like me.

Use it like a superpower, and get intentional. You have 8 games. Which one right now lights you up the most as a gut reaction. That’s the one to pour your attention into.

This is where it gets fun. Slice out your hook. What about that game makes it fun. Focus there. Make it feel good. Now make it feel even better. Not just the art. The camera. The vfx. The sounds. All of it. Then share it. The most exciting parts. Do people respond to it? If not, explore why and try something else. Still nothing? You have 7 more seeds to plant.

No more ideas. Go water one.

replies.author: Junior_Muffin5931
replies.body: I have ADHD and autism lol. So yeah I do. But I agree. That is why all these games are in various stages of development. My warehouse gig pays me decently so I can pay for the 200 plan for Claude and the 100 plan for Chatgpt.

replies.author: StaticAnchor
replies.body:
And you don’t even need all that. I’m only running $20 Claude.

For the game you pick, fight the urge to go big. Go small. Idk what genres or kinds of games you are trying to make exactly, but literally build an interesting mechanic and atmosphere. What sort of vision do you want to share with people. What’s something familiar but unique about your game. Focus on that hook, and share it. If people fuck with it, there’s your greenlight to build.

I’m working on a lookdev studio that helps with this that I’m sharing next week, happy to send it your way once it’s ready.

replies.author: Junior_Muffin5931
replies.body: For one game, sure, $20 would do it. I'm running hourly coding sessions across multiple projects every day while I'm at work, plus native ports where every function gets checked against the original. That burns through limits fast, and I still max out the $200 plan. And yeah, send the lookdev studio my way when it's ready, I'd like to see it.

replies.author: FireRapper
replies.body:
Before building more games, I think it would be a much better use of your time to build a universal telemetry dashboard that you can integrate across your games. Something that lets you track where players drop off, reconstruct what they experienced, and identify device-specific performance issues. You could use GPT to create the detailed specifications and Claude to build it.

Nothing wrong with being ambitious, and you’ve already taken a huge step by building a community early. But one thing I’ve learned from developing my own game is how differently regular players interact with a game compared to how its developer expects them to. Having that level of insight before investing heavily in multiple games could save you hundreds of hours of development and help you manage your expectations.

replies.author: Junior_Muffin5931
replies.body: Appreciate it, genuinely. APD is the one I'm pouring into, it launches January 1 and it's the one I play every day. The rest move slower on purpose and none of them ship until they feel right on my own phone.

replies.author: Previous_Host_9990
replies.body:
100% - I'm exactly in this boat and recently prompted my AI of choice "Remove all these other steam pages and itch builds. Until I ship Tooth and Tusk (https://nbd2.itch.io/tooth-and-tusk coming NextFest spring 27) you are not allowed to do meaningful work on anything else" ... Not because my other ideas are bad, or even because this idea is very good. 

But building and ideating is the fun part, but that's not where minds like OP and myself need to grow. We need to grow in focus, polish, completion, marketing, etc. if we want to deliver games that matter. Otherwise it'll be an endless string of "could be cool" prototypes that no one truly enjoys (except the person building it - because it is genuinely fun and addicting).

replies.author: StaticAnchor
replies.body: I’m the same way, honestly. It’s only hit me in the recent weeks that you can still iterate, just within the context of your own game. It changed everything for me, and you can still explore and build and make your own game juicier. It might be even more fun than the different ideas. I can’t believe I just wrote that lol.
